title: What is Media Bias?
description: Partisan, structural, commercial, cognitive — distinguishing kinds of bias

concepts.title: Bias: A Useful Word, Used Loosely
concepts.contentHtml:
"Media bias" is one of the most-used and least-precise terms in popular debate about journalism. Pressed for a definition, most people mean some combination of: not telling the whole story, treating my side unfairly, covering some stories and not others, and using loaded language. Each is a real phenomenon; they are not the same phenomenon.

Media scholars typically split bias into several distinguishable kinds. Partisan bias: systematic favouritism toward one political side in story selection, framing, or commentary. Structural bias: the patterns built into news production itself — pack journalism, dependence on official sources, the preference for novelty over routine — which produce predictable distortions even from individually fair-minded reporters. Commercial bias: the pull of stories that sell or score well on engagement, which favours conflict, celebrity, and crime over policy detail. Cognitive bias: the influence of reporters' and editors' own social and professional backgrounds on what they notice and what they take for granted.

Most empirical work on bias finds that all four operate, that they sometimes pull in opposite directions, and that no single number can capture them. The complaint that "the media" is biased without specifying which bias and against what usually does not survive close inspection. The interesting question is not whether bias exists — it inevitably does — but which biases dominate which outlets at which moments, and how readers can compensate.

concepts.title: Measuring Bias: From Slant Scores to Audience Studies
concepts.contentHtml:
Quantitative work on partisan bias has matured substantially. Tim Groseclose and Jeffrey Milyo's 2005 paper in the Quarterly Journal of Economics measured congressional citations by think tanks of various ideological scores, then matched outlets to think tanks they cited; the resulting "ADA score" placed most major US outlets to the left of the median voter, with Fox News Special Report as a clear conservative outlier. Matthew Gentzkow and Jesse Shapiro (2010) built a different measure based on the rates at which outlets used distinctively Democratic or Republican phrases.

European work has used similar techniques on UK and German outlets, generally finding less partisan slant on news pages than on opinion pages, and less in public-service broadcasters than in commercial outlets. The deeper finding is that most newspapers' slant matches the politics of their audiences — Gentzkow and Shapiro's evidence suggests this is largely a market response, not an ideological project.

Audience studies tell another part of the story. Vavreck and Iyengar's polarisation work, Jonathan Ladd's research on declining trust in media, and Pew's long-running surveys all show that Americans now consume news heavily filtered by political identity and that perceptions of bias often run ahead of measurable partisan content. Studies of so-called hostile media effect (Vallone, Ross, and Lepper, 1985) show partisans on opposite sides of an issue can both rate the same news report as biased against them — a finding that complicates claims of objective measurement.

concepts.title: Bias, Balance, and the False-Equivalence Trap
concepts.contentHtml:
The traditional newsroom response to bias accusations has been a discipline of balance: present both sides of contested questions, give equal time to spokespersons of opposing views, and refrain from editorialising in news copy. The discipline has real value — it pushes reporters to test their assumptions and prevents the most flagrant partisan abuses.

It also has well-known failure modes. False equivalence arises when balance is applied to questions where the evidence is asymmetric: covering climate science by giving equal time to a climate scientist and a paid sceptic, or covering a candidate's lies by "both-sidesing" them with a comparable list from the opponent. Jay Rosen and others have argued that this kind of automatic balance produces its own distortion — a more subtle bias toward whichever side is more willing to lie or exaggerate.

The contemporary alternative being pursued by some major outlets — the Washington Post's "Democracy Dies in Darkness" era, the BBC's reviews of impartiality after Brexit and Covid coverage — is to insist that truth is a higher journalistic value than balance. Where the evidence is genuinely contested, present both sides. Where it is not, say so. The shift is contested in turn: critics call it abandoned objectivity; defenders argue it is the recovery of older norms (Kovach and Rosenstiel's "discipline of verification") from a balance practice that had decayed into reflex. Both arguments are alive in every working newsroom.

title: Framing Theory
description: Goffman, Entman — how the same facts produce different stories

concepts.title: What Framing Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Framing is the selection of certain aspects of a perceived reality and the highlighting of those aspects in a text in such a way as to promote a particular interpretation. The most-cited modern definition is Robert Entman's in his 1993 essay "Framing: Toward Clarification of a Fractured Paradigm": frames define problems, diagnose causes, make moral judgments, and suggest remedies.

The intellectual ancestry runs through the sociologist Erving Goffman's Frame Analysis (1974), which argued that ordinary social interaction depends on tacitly shared frames that tell participants what kind of situation they are in. Journalism inherits the same machinery: a story about a protest can be framed as "citizens demanding accountability" or as "rioters disrupting public order," using the same underlying events and many of the same words.

Frames operate at several levels at once. Word choice: insurgents vs militants vs freedom fighters vs terrorists. Story structure: leading with police statements vs leading with eyewitness accounts. Visual selection: photographs of crowds shouting vs photographs of crowds singing. Source choice: whom you call for comment, and in what order, signals what kind of story you are telling. None of this is necessarily dishonest; all of it is unavoidable; and all of it is consequential.

concepts.title: Famous Examples
concepts.contentHtml:
The classic empirical demonstration is Shanto Iyengar's work on episodic vs thematic framing of social problems. Episodic frames present poverty, crime, or unemployment through the story of an individual; thematic frames present them through aggregate trends and structural causes. Iyengar's experiments showed that audiences exposed to episodic framing tended to attribute responsibility to individuals — "why didn't they get a job?" — while audiences exposed to thematic framing pointed to systemic causes. The frame, more than the underlying facts, shaped the political interpretation.

Other famous instances. The choice between "estate tax" and "death tax" — the same policy, different frames — was reshaped in US politics partly through deliberate Republican message discipline (Frank Luntz's polling work). The framing of the 2003 Iraq invasion as "regime change" vs "illegal war" produced very different baseline coverage in different countries. The framing of climate change as "scientific debate" vs "scientific consensus with political resistance" substantially shifted in major outlets between 2005 and 2015 and reshaped public understanding accordingly.

The point is not that any frame is uniquely correct. It is that frames carry consequences for how audiences attribute responsibility, what policies they consider plausible, and which actors they regard as legitimate. Reporters cannot avoid framing; they can become more conscious of it.

concepts.title: Frame Disputes and Counter-Frames
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most consistent findings in framing research is that frames once established are sticky. Once a story is framed in a particular way — "welfare queen," "war on terror," "migrant crisis," "Big Tech" — that frame organises subsequent coverage in ways that are hard to dislodge. Counter-frames take effort, repetition, and their own institutional backing to compete. George Lakoff's influential work in cognitive linguistics argues that progressives in the US lost decades of policy battles partly because they accepted right-wing frames (taxes as a burden, regulation as red tape) on their opponents' own terms.

Modern political campaigns and corporate communications take framing seriously enough to invest heavily in it. Spin doctors, "narrative strategists," opposition research, and crisis-communications consultants are all in the business of frame management. The shift from a press that produced its own frames to a press that often relays frames produced by professional sources is one of the structural changes the framing literature has tracked since the 1990s.

The defensive practice for working journalists is to name frames explicitly: to write as though the choice of frame is a piece of the story to be reported on, not just a tool to be used. Daniel Hallin's "spheres of consensus, legitimate controversy, and deviance" (1986) is one classical schema for thinking about which frames a newsroom currently takes for granted. The map of those spheres shifts over time; the journalist's job is partly to notice when it has shifted, and to make those shifts visible to readers.

title: Agenda-Setting
description: McCombs & Shaw — the press tells us not what to think but what to think about

concepts.title: The Chapel Hill Study and Agenda-Setting
concepts.contentHtml:
Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw's 1968 study of undecided voters in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, during the US presidential campaign, is the founding study of agenda-setting theory. The researchers compared the issues voters said were most important to them with the issues local news media had covered most heavily; the correlation was strikingly high, even when actual political content of those stories varied. The voters' agendas tracked the press's agendas.

The thesis crystallised in Bernard Cohen's often-quoted 1963 line: the press "may not be successful much of the time in telling people what to think, but it is stunningly successful in telling its readers what to think about." The strong claim of agenda-setting research is not that media tell audiences what positions to hold, but that media shape the salience of issues — which questions count as urgent, which as routine, which as not worth discussing at all.

Subsequent decades of empirical work have largely supported and refined the thesis. The size of agenda-setting effects varies with audience attention, partisan strength, and issue type (issues people experience directly — gas prices, schools — show smaller media effects than issues they only learn about through media). But the general finding has held up well across methods and across countries.

concepts.title: Second-Level Agenda-Setting and Priming
concepts.contentHtml:
The original theory addressed only the salience of issues. Second-level agenda-setting extends it to the salience of attributes: not just whether the public thinks about the economy, but which features of the economy (unemployment, inflation, growth, inequality) come to mind. McCombs's later work and the European studies that followed treat second-level agenda-setting as conceptually close to framing — different vocabularies for related phenomena.

The closely related concept is priming, developed by Iyengar, Kinder, and Peters in the 1980s. Priming holds that by elevating certain issues, media change the criteria by which audiences evaluate political actors. If coverage emphasises foreign policy in the weeks before an election, voters will judge candidates more by foreign-policy performance; if it emphasises the economy, by economic performance. Politicians, of course, know this, which is why so much of campaigning is the attempt to set the agenda the public will use to judge them.

Note what these effects are not. Agenda-setting and priming are not subliminal manipulation; they operate in plain view. Audiences are not coerced into thinking about what the press covers — they have the option to ignore the news entirely — but for those who do follow the news, the issues they take to be important are powerfully influenced by which stories appear on the front page or in the top of the broadcast.

concepts.title: Agenda-Setting in the Algorithmic Era
concepts.contentHtml:
The agenda-setting literature was developed in the era of mass media — three TV networks, a few major newspapers, broad shared exposure to the same set of stories. The fragmentation of media in the 2000s and the rise of algorithmic feeds in the 2010s have reshaped the picture.

Two consequences are most discussed. First, the aggregator set of platforms — Google News, Facebook, Twitter/X, TikTok, YouTube — now acts as a powerful intermediary agenda-setter. Their ranking algorithms determine, for billions of users, which stories rise and which sink. Studies of YouTube and TikTok recommendation systems have shown that the algorithms do not just reflect user interest but shape it, with significant feedback effects.

Second, the agenda has become more fragmented and personalised. The same election or war is covered through different prisms in different platform niches; partisans on opposite sides may now disagree not only about how to interpret events but about which events count as events. Yochai Benkler, Robert Faris, and Hal Roberts's Network Propaganda (2018) documented how the right-wing media ecosystem in the US increasingly operated as a separate agenda-setting universe with its own internal logic. The classical agenda-setting effect — a single shared agenda imposed on a national audience — has not disappeared but has been overlaid by multiple, parallel agendas competing for influence within audience subsets.

title: Selection, Omission & Gatekeeping
description: What gets covered, what doesn't, and who decides

concepts.title: Mr. Gates and the Gatekeeper Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
The first systematic empirical study of how news is selected was David Manning White's 1950 paper "The 'Gate Keeper': A Case Study in the Selection of News." White followed an Iowa wire editor he called "Mr. Gates," recording every story Gates rejected and his reasons. The result was a portrait of news selection as massively subtractive: of the thousands of items moving through the wire each week, only a fraction made it into the paper, and the cut was driven by the editor's tacit sense of newsworthiness.

The gatekeeper tradition that grew from White's study has been refined repeatedly. The Norwegian researchers Galtung and Ruge (1965) tried to identify the dimensions of newsworthiness empirically, listing twelve criteria including frequency, magnitude, unambiguity, cultural proximity, unexpectedness, and elite involvement. Later work (Harcup and O'Neill, 2001, 2017) has updated the list for the digital era, adding shareability and audience metrics.

The general finding is consistent: news is not a representative sample of what happens in the world. A small number of elite countries, institutions, and individuals receive coverage out of all proportion to their share of population or even of significant events. Whole regions go uncovered for years; trends that don't fit a story arc go unreported until a single dramatic event makes them visible. The gates open and close along well-documented lines.

concepts.title: Routine Bias and the Sociology of News Production
concepts.contentHtml:
The sociologists who came of age in the 1970s — Herbert Gans, Gaye Tuchman, Mark Fishman — moved beyond individual gatekeepers to the structure of news production itself. Their finding was that newsroom routines, designed for efficiency, produce predictable distortions even when individual journalists are scrupulously fair.

Gans's Deciding What's News (1979) showed that the major US networks and newsmagazines covered remarkably similar stories week after week, drawing on a shared map of who counts as a relevant source: high officials, business leaders, established experts, and a small list of recurring institutions. Tuchman's Making News (1978) traced the "news net" — the system of beats, regular sources, and predictable events (court rulings, scheduled press conferences) — and showed that anything outside the net was systematically less likely to be covered. Fishman's Manufacturing the News (1980) made a related case from local crime reporting.

The implication is that what readers and viewers experience as "the news" is in important part a function of which institutional rhythms generate stories cheaply and which do not. State legislatures, police-beat blotters, and the State Department generate news on schedule; community organisations, structural economic shifts, and the consequences of long-running policy decisions do not. Reporters who try to break out of the routines have to work much harder against the structural pull of the news net.

concepts.title: Omission, the Missing Story, and the Market Failure
concepts.contentHtml:
The most consequential bias is often what is not covered. The annual Project Censored report, the work of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, and academic studies of "news deserts" document the gaps. Local accountability journalism in the US has collapsed: roughly one-third of US newspapers that existed in 2005 have closed, and over 200 US counties had no local news outlet at all by 2024 — a phenomenon documented in detail by Penny Abernathy, first at UNC's Hussman School and since 2020 at Northwestern's Medill School. International coverage in Western media has shrunk by similar percentages.

The structural explanation is the collapse of advertising-funded local journalism (covered in this domain's media-economics topic). Without commercial backing, the routine accountability beat — local courts, school boards, county commissions — goes uncovered. Studies (Hayes and Lawless, Schulhofer-Wohl and Garrido) have linked the closure of local newspapers to declines in voter turnout, weaker oversight of local government, and increases in municipal borrowing costs.

The contemporary responses are partial. Non-profit local news — The Texas Tribune, City Bureau, The Marshall Project, ProPublica Local — has reached scale in some areas but cannot yet replace lost commercial coverage. Public-service expansion via the BBC's local democracy reporters and similar initiatives has stabilised some markets. Foundation-funded reporting and academic-journalism partnerships have helped at the high end. None of these replaces the basic question: who decides what gets covered, and on whose dime? Selection bias is not a personal failing of reporters but a structural property of the system that produces journalism — and the structure has changed substantially in the past two decades.

title: Partisan Press & Echo Chambers
description: Fox, MSNBC, GB News, talk radio — the modern partisan ecosystem

concepts.title: From Mass Press to Partisan Cable
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of the 20th century, mainstream US journalism was self-consciously non-partisan — at least at the level of straight news. The norm was an artefact of postwar conditions: three TV networks, a few wire agencies that needed to sell to politically diverse papers, and a regulatory regime (notably the Fairness Doctrine, enforced 1949–1987) that obliged broadcasters to present opposing views on controversial issues.

Two decisions in the late 1980s changed the picture. The FCC repealed the Fairness Doctrine in 1987 under the Reagan administration, freeing AM radio in particular to broadcast unrebutted partisan opinion. Rush Limbaugh's national syndication began in 1988; conservative talk radio became a major political force across the 1990s. The 1996 Telecommunications Act loosened ownership rules and accelerated cable-news growth.

The pattern visible by the 2000s — Fox News (1996) on the right, MSNBC drifting toward an explicit progressive stance through the 2000s, talk radio dominated by conservatives, and online ecosystems forming distinct partisan habitats — has shaped US politics ever since. Britain's broadly non-partisan postwar broadcast environment held longer (the BBC and ITN as the dominant news providers) but has been visibly under pressure since the 2010s with GB News (2021) and TalkTV (2022) modelling themselves on Fox-style partisan opinion broadcasting.

concepts.title: Echo Chambers, Filter Bubbles, and What the Evidence Says
concepts.contentHtml:
Two related concepts dominate popular discussion of contemporary partisan media. The echo chamber (Cass Sunstein and others) is a self-reinforcing media environment where consumers encounter mostly opinions they already hold. The filter bubble (Eli Pariser, 2011) is the personalised informational environment created by algorithmic curation, narrowing what users see based on inferred preferences.

The empirical evidence is more nuanced than the popular framing suggests. Studies by Andrew Guess, Brendan Nyhan, and others have repeatedly found that:

  • Most consumers in democracies still have more diverse news diets than the strong echo-chamber thesis predicts.
  • Partisan news consumption is concentrated in a relatively small but politically active minority — perhaps 5–15% of the public — whose effects on the broader information environment are disproportionate to their share of attention.
  • Social-media platforms can increase exposure to cross-cutting views in some configurations and reduce it in others; the algorithmic effect is not monolithic.

The deeper structural change is the parallel ecosystems documented by Yochai Benkler, Robert Faris, and Hal Roberts in Network Propaganda (2018). They mapped the US right-wing media universe and found it operating largely as a self-contained ecosystem with its own internal logic, distinct from the broader American media environment. Whether echo chambers are widespread is debated; that distinct partisan media ecosystems exist is not.

concepts.title: Polarisation, Trust, and the Cost
concepts.contentHtml:
The cumulative effect of partisan media on public life is one of the most debated questions in contemporary political science. Affective polarisation — the phenomenon where partisans feel growing dislike and distrust of the other side, even more than they disagree on policy — has risen sharply in the US since the 1990s and in many European democracies more recently. Shanto Iyengar's research suggests that partisan-media diet is one (not the only) significant predictor of affective polarisation.

Trust in media has dropped in tandem. US Gallup polling shows trust in mass media falling from around 70% in the early 1970s to a record low around 31% by 2024. The decline is sharpest among Republicans (around 12% in recent surveys), while Democrats remain comparatively higher. The pattern across OECD democracies is broadly similar in direction but less extreme.

The chain is not perfectly clear. Partisan media benefits from polarisation — programmes that reliably anger their audience perform better — and may help drive it; but causation runs in multiple directions, with social media, demographic shifts, and party realignment all part of the picture. The defensive responses — non-profit local journalism, public-service broadcasting, audience-funded subscription models that reward verification over outrage — exist but operate at much smaller scale than the partisan-attention economy. Whether the trend reverses in the coming decade or deepens into permanent fracture is one of the central political questions of the period.

title: Measuring Bias Empirically
description: Content analysis, slant scores, audience surveys — quantitative approaches

concepts.title: Content Analysis: The Workhorse Method
concepts.contentHtml:
The oldest and most flexible method for studying media bias is content analysis: the systematic coding of large bodies of text or video against an explicit coding scheme. Bernard Berelson's Content Analysis in Communication Research (1952) gave the method its modern foundations.

The basic procedure is unchanged across decades. Researchers define a population of coverage (e.g. front-page election stories from a set of newspapers over a campaign), draw a sample, develop a coding scheme (favourable/neutral/unfavourable mentions; presence of specific frames; source diversity), and have multiple coders apply the scheme with reliability checks. The output is quantitative data on which patterns can be tested.

Content analysis is laborious but produces the most defensible empirical claims about coverage. Studies of tone in election coverage (Patterson's work on US presidential races), of source diversity in foreign reporting, of visual framing of social movements, and of topic balance on cable news all use variations of the technique. The 21st-century innovation is computational content analysis — supervised machine-learning classifiers, topic models, and (since 2022) large-language-model coding — which has dramatically expanded the volume of text that can be analysed at the cost of some interpretive depth.

concepts.title: Slant Measures and Indirect Estimation
concepts.contentHtml:
A second family of techniques tries to measure partisan slant indirectly, by exploiting external benchmarks. Tim Groseclose and Jeffrey Milyo's 2005 QJE paper measured how often US news outlets cited the same think tanks that members of Congress cited, then used the citing legislators' ADA scores (a left-right rating) to assign each outlet a position on the same scale. Most major outlets came out left of the median voter; Fox News Special Report emerged as a clear conservative outlier.

Matthew Gentzkow and Jesse Shapiro's 2010 Econometrica paper built a different measure based on the rates at which outlets used distinctively Democratic or Republican phrases — "estate tax" vs "death tax", "undocumented immigrants" vs "illegal aliens." They then tested whether outlet slant matched ownership or audience and found a much stronger fit with audience: the partisan slant of US newspapers is largely a market response to readers' politics rather than imposed by owners.

Indirect measures have known limits. They depend on the validity of the external benchmark; they can miss bias that is structural rather than partisan; and they are sensitive to which phrases or sources count as "distinctive." But they have become a standard part of the empirical-bias toolkit, and their results have been broadly stable: most measurable partisan slant in major US media tracks the politics of the audience that pays for the outlet.

concepts.title: Audience Surveys, Field Experiments, and the New Frontier
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond content, researchers measure bias through audience surveys and field experiments. The Reuters Institute Digital News Report, Pew's media surveys, and the European Broadcasting Union's audience studies all track who consumes which outlets, what they trust, and how cross-cutting their news diets are. Surveys reveal not what coverage is but what audiences perceive; the gap is itself informative — the hostile media effect tells you partisans on opposite sides of an issue often see the same coverage as biased against them.

Field experiments are more powerful where they are feasible. Allcott et al. (2020) paid Facebook users to deactivate their accounts for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterms; the deactivated group showed reduced political polarisation but also reduced political knowledge. Levy (2021) randomly assigned users to follow either a left-wing or a right-wing news source on Facebook, finding effects on political attitudes that varied by initial partisan position. These are some of the cleanest causal estimates of partisan-media effects available.

The new methodological frontier is large-language-model coding of media content at scale, with cross-platform tracking of how stories migrate between outlets. The catch is reproducibility: many of the most interesting recent studies depend on platform data that the platforms have since restricted (Twitter/X's API changes after 2022, Meta's CrowdTangle shutdown in 2024). Empirical work on media bias is therefore in an ironic position: better tools, more data than ever, and increasingly limited access to the platforms that now mediate most political information.
